newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Italy to gain from EMU's latest twist.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Italy to gain from EMU's latest twist.

text.p: Italian government bonds hold promise for investors as the European Economic and Monetary Union saga takes yet another twist with speculation of a softer approach to the Maastricht criteria, analysts said on Monday.

During a meeting of European finance ministers in the Netherlands over the weekend, British newspapers reported German Finance Minister Theo Waigel as saying he had "never nailed himself to the cross of three percent."
Waigel, and other German ministers have since denied any weakening of the deficit criteria.

"The market is obsessed with the whole discussion about how strictly the criteria should be applied," said Han de Jong, head of bond research at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam. "It is a little bit over played."
He was doubtful about how much loss of credibility in EMU would actually pertain to a failure to meet the deficit target.

"Politicians are making clear that they want EMU to go ahead and on time, and with the participation of as many countries as possible," he said. "The route being taken is to be as strict as you can for the time being and then at the end of the day you can soften a bit or allow for countries to fudge a bit."
Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch in London, said what was important about Waigel's comments was not what he said but the interpretation of what he meant.

"The market will see any slippage of the three percent criteria as increasing the chances of a broad EMU," he said. It was becoming increasingly difficult for Germany to reach the three percent deficit, he said because additional fiscal tightening in Germany was not politically acceptable.
"It is possible that Waigel's comments accept an appreciation of that," Islam said.

Julian Jessop, European economist at Nikko Europe in London, said while the next turn in market sentiment would be towards the idea of a soft monetary union, a broad monetary union would be unacceptable to the German public.

"It is clear that they are taking two steps forwards and one step back towards a more flexible position," he said. "That view is no better than neutral for core markets, but the flip side of it is that it is positive for Italy."
Jessop said he would be bullish on Italy across the curve.
"The EMU talk is likely to favour the long end of the market but you've also got positive expectations about interest rate cuts which will help the short end," he said.

The 10-year BTP/Bund yield spread had narrowed to 176 basis points by 1017 GMT from 181 at Friday's close. The gap pushed over 200 basis points in mid-March dogged by market concerns about a delay to the start of EMU.
De Jong said the potential was for the gap to narrow further over the next few months. "If the market gets a bit enthusiastic it could easily go back to the 150 or 140 level," he said.
Islam also said further convergence was likely but would be driven by rising yields in the mark bloc rather than a significant further fall in 10-year yields in Italy and Spain.
"There is an upwards risk to yields globally in the 10-year area," he said. "But on a fundamental view a case can be made at the short end of Italy."

He said two-year yields were currently above money rates and the rebound on the dollar should be accompanied by a further recovery of the lira, which in turn would be supportive of establishing outright long positions at the short end of Italy.
Jessop said the move in EMU sentiment might also be potentially positive for British gilts, which investors could use as a safe haven.
"But I am a little bit wary of piling into the UK when it is only a few weeks before the election."
